synopsis: Decades of imperial vanity, naval rivalries, and rigid alliance treaties wound the clockwork of European catastrophe. From the blood and iron of German unification under Bismarck to the industrial race between British Dreadnoughts and Kaiser Wilhelm’s High Seas Fleet, Europe split into two heavily armed camps. When a teenage assassin fired two fatal shots in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914, thirty days of diplomatic brinkmanship sleepwalked an entire continent into total war.

stages.title: Prussian Rise & "Blood and Iron"
stages.trigger: Chief Minister Otto von Bismarck uses military expansion and short wars against Denmark and Austria to unite northern German states under Prussian dominance.
stages.connective: Shattered the traditional European balance of power, deeply alarming France who feared a powerful united neighbour on its eastern border.
stages.question: How did Bismarck’s "Blood and Iron" policy make Prussia dominant?

stages.title: The Battle of Sedan & French Defeat
stages.trigger: Prussian armies encircle the French army at Sedan, capturing Emperor Napoleon III and 100,000 troops in a crushing French defeat.
stages.connective: Toppled the French imperial government, leaving Paris under siege and compelling southern German states to join the new Empire.
stages.question: How did defeat at Sedan lead to the 1871 German Empire at Versailles?

stages.title: Hall of Mirrors & Alsace-Lorraine Seized
stages.trigger: Wilhelm I is proclaimed German Kaiser in Versailles' Hall of Mirrors; Germany annexes mineral-rich Alsace-Lorraine and imposes a 5 billion franc indemnity.
stages.connective: Inflicted deep national humiliation on France, creating permanent resentment and an unshakeable national obsession with revenge.
stages.question: Why did the 1871 Treaty of Frankfurt create bitter hatred in France?

stages.title: The Cult of French "Revanche"
stages.trigger: French schools, politics, and culture rally around "Revanche" (revenge)—a national determination to reclaim Alsace-Lorraine from Germany.
stages.connective: Convinced German leaders that France was a permanent enemy who would attack the moment an alliance was formed.
stages.question: How did French schools and conscription prepare youth for revanche?

stages.title: Bismarck's Web & Two-Front Dread
stages.trigger: Bismarck constructs complex treaties (Dual Alliance, Reinsurance Treaty) to keep France isolated and avoid a two-front war with Russia.
stages.connective: Maintained fragile peace until Wilhelm II abandoned Russia in 1890, opening the door for rival European alliance blocs.
stages.question: How did Bismarck’s 1887 treaty with Russia keep France isolated?

video.title: The Franco Prussian War - History Matters (Short Animated Documentary)
video.teacher_guidance: Fast animated breakdown of Otto von Bismarck's diplomacy, the Ems Dispatch, the defeat of Napoleon III at Sedan in 1870, and the proclamation of the German Empire in Versailles. Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–03:30 • Lesson Phase: Quick Starter Check (0–3m). Tone Alert: Fast, accessible animated educational summary.
video.viewing_task:
1. [01:10] Quick Check: In which palace's Hall of Mirrors did the German princes proclaim King Wilhelm I of Prussia as German Emperor (Kaiser) on 18 January 1871?
  2. [02:40] Hinge Question: Why did the German annexation of the French border provinces of Alsace and Lorraine guarantee permanent French hostility and revanchism leading up to 1914?
video.model_answer:
1. Quick Check: The Palace of Versailles, near Paris.
  2. Hinge Question: Annexing Alsace-Lorraine was seen in France as a humiliating violation of French national sovereignty. Generations of French schoolchildren were taught to gaze eastward at the "lost provinces" draped in black mourning, creating an unshakeable French determination for revenge (revanche) and guaranteeing that France would ally with any power hostile to Germany.

video.title: German Unification and Empire - History in 5 Minutes
video.teacher_guidance: Examines Otto von Bismarck's strategy of "Blood and Iron", the three wars of unification (Denmark 1864, Austria 1866, France 1870), and how unified Germany disrupted the European balance of power. Recommended Watch Window: 00:45–04:45 • Lesson Phase: Guided Instruction & Archival Investigation. Tone Alert: Structured historical overview exploring the European balance of power.
video.viewing_task:
1. [01:30] Recall: What famous phrase did Chancellor Otto von Bismarck use in 1862 to declare that the great questions of the day would be resolved not by speeches and majority resolutions, but by military force?
  2. [03:15] Explain: Explain how Chancellor Bismarck's complex network of alliances (such as the 1879 Dual Alliance and 1887 Reinsurance Treaty) sought to keep France diplomatically isolated and prevent a two-front war.
  3. [04:20] Challenge: Evaluate how Kaiser Wilhelm II's dismissal of Bismarck in 1890 and abandonment of the Reinsurance Treaty allowed France to break out of isolation by signing the 1894 Franco-Russian Alliance.
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: "Blood and Iron" (Eisen und Blut).
  2. Explain: Bismarck understood that Germany's central European geography made it vulnerable to encirclement. He prioritized maintaining friendly relations with Russia and Austria-Hungary while keeping France isolated without great power allies, ensuring France could never mount a war of revenge to recover Alsace-Lorraine.
  3. Challenge: Kaiser Wilhelm II foolishly allowed the secret Reinsurance Treaty with Tsarist Russia to lapse, believing dynamic British ties would compensate. Deprived of German diplomatic support and needing capital loans, autocratic Russia allied with republican France in 1894, creating Bismarck's ultimate nightmare: a hostile military coalition encircling Germany on both its western and eastern frontiers.

video.title: How Prussia Ended The French Empire: Franco-Prussian War | Animated History
video.teacher_guidance: In-depth tactical and strategic analysis by The Armchair Historian: Prussian needle-guns, rail logistics, Krupp breech-loading artillery, and the Siege of Paris. Recommended Watch Window: 01:30–08:00 • Lesson Phase: High-Attainer Stretch & Military Analysis. Tone Alert: Deep military and technological history.
video.viewing_task:
1. [03:00] Recall: At which decisive frontier fortress did Field Marshal Helmuth von Moltke encircle Emperor Napoleon III and 100,000 French soldiers in September 1870?
  2. [05:30] Explain: How did Prussian mastery of modern railway mobilization and Krupp steel rifled artillery revolutionize 19th-century European warfare?
  3. [07:15] Challenge: Analyze the siege of Paris (September 1870–January 1871) and the Paris Commune: how did civilian suffering and revolutionary uprising intensify Franco-German hatred?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The Battle of Sedan.
  2. Explain: The Prussian General Staff used comprehensive railway timetables to mobilize hundreds of thousands of reservists to the frontier in days, far outstripping French preparations. Furthermore, Krupp steel breech-loading cannons had twice the range and rate of fire of French bronze muzzle-loaders, allowing Prussian batteries to destroy French positions from beyond retaliatory range.
  3. Challenge: Prussian bombardment and the starvation of Paris (where citizens were reduced to eating horses, dogs, and zoo animals) created deep psychological trauma. When the revolutionary Paris Commune was subsequently crushed with 20,000 French deaths, French society blamed Prussian militarism for tearing their nation apart, cementing generational enmity.

video.title: "The Great War" 1 | What Made Germany So Successful Before World War 1?
video.teacher_guidance: Authoritative archival documentary exploring Germany's explosive economic expansion between 1871 and 1914: steel production overtaking Britain, chemical dominance, and population growth. Recommended Watch Window: 02:00–07:30 • Lesson Phase: Guided Instruction & Economic Deconstruction. Tone Alert: Scholarly archival documentary.
video.viewing_task:
1. [03:15] Recall: By 1914, by how much had unified Germany's steel production overtaken that of Great Britain, the original "workshop of the world"?
  2. [05:10] Explain: Describe how Germany's world-leading electrical, chemical, and precision engineering sectors created a sense of national invincibility and technological superiority.
  3. [07:00] Challenge: Evaluate how rapid German industrialization created domestic political tension between the conservative Junker military aristocracy and the rising socialist working-class SPD electorate.
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: Germany produced over 17 million tons of steel annually by 1914, more than double Great Britain's 7.6 million tons.
  2. Explain: German chemical conglomerates like Bayer, BASF, and Hoechst produced over 80% of the world's synthetic dyes, pharmaceuticals, and industrial fertilizers, while engineering giants like Siemens and AEG dominated global electrical infrastructure, fostering imperial confidence that German science and industry were destined to dominate Europe.
  3. Challenge: While heavy industry made Germany an economic superpower, political power remained concentrated in the autocratic Kaiser and aristocratic Prussian military elite. As the socialist SPD grew into the largest party in the Reichstag, conservative elites feared socialist revolution at home, viewing aggressive imperial foreign policy and military expansion as a way to rally patriotic national unity and neutralize working-class dissent.

lessons.skill: Change & Continuity: Balance of Power & Revanche
lessons.title: Enquiry 1: German Unification, Franco-Prussian War & Bismarck (1871–1890)
lessons.subtitle: From Blood & Iron to the Hall of Mirrors and the Seizure of Alsace-Lorraine
lessons.enquiryQuestion: How did German unification in 1871 unsettle the balance of power in Europe?

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry introduces students to the foundational geopolitical shockwave of modern European history: the creation of a unified, militaristic German Empire in 1871. Students examine how Otto von Bismarck used three calculated wars to unite 39 sovereign states under Prussian dominance, culminated in the coronation of Kaiser Wilhelm I inside the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, and provoked permanent French hostility through the annexation of Alsace-Lorraine. The enquiry concludes by examining Bismarck’s intricate web of defensive alliances designed to isolate France and prevent Germany’s strategic nightmare: a two-front encirclement.

objectives.objective: Understand how Otto von Bismarck used 'blood and iron' and the Franco-Prussian War to unify the German states.
objectives.primer: Focus on paragraphs [1.1] and [1.2]. Emphasize that Bismarck rejected liberal parliamentary democracy in favor of military force, railway mobilization, and Krupp steel artillery.
objectives.question: What did Bismarck mean by 'iron and blood', and why did crowning the Kaiser at Versailles deliberately humiliate France?

objectives.objective: Analyze why the annexation of Alsace-Lorraine created permanent French 'Revanche' and shattered the European balance of power.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraphs [1.3] and [1.4] alongside Bettannier’s painting 'La Tache Noire'. Show how losing border fortress cities and coalfields turned revenge into a civic religion.
objectives.question: Why was the annexation of Alsace-Lorraine a far more dangerous penalty than the 5 billion gold franc indemnity?

objectives.objective: Evaluate how Bismarck's post-1871 alliance system sought to prevent a two-front encirclement.
objectives.primer: Focus on paragraph [1.5]. Explain Gordon Craig’s paradox: seizing Alsace-Lorraine gave Germany fortified borders but trapped it in permanent strategic paranoia.
objectives.question: Why was maintaining friendship with Russia Bismarck’s supreme foreign policy rule after 1871?

source_context.Source A: The unification of Germany in 1871 shattered the traditional balance of power established at the Congress of Vienna in 1815. In place of a fragmented buffer zone of weak German principalities, a single industrial and military titan emerged at the heart of Europe. **Hinge Question:** Why did the sudden creation of a unified, industrialized Germany in Central Europe inherently threaten the strategic security of both France and Russia?
source_context.Source B: Following the catastrophic French defeat at Sedan, Bismarck orchestrated the coronation of Kaiser Wilhelm I inside the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles—the historic palace of French royalty and power. This deliberate humiliation of France on its own soil ignited an enduring desire for national revenge (revanche). **Hinge Question:** How did staging the German coronation inside the French Palace of Versailles transform a military defeat into an irreconcilable national feud?
source_context.Source C: Under the Treaty of Frankfurt, Germany annexed the mineral-rich provinces of Alsace and eastern Lorraine without a plebiscite and forced France to pay a staggering 5 billion gold franc indemnity. This treaty created a permanent grievance in French political life. **Hinge Question:** Why did the seizure of Alsace-Lorraine guarantee that Franco-German relations could never be genuinely normalized under Bismarck?
source_context.Source D: Following 1871, the French Third Republic mobilized the state education system to keep the memory of the 'lost provinces' alive. Schoolboys were instructed in military drill, gymnastics, and patriotic history under the doctrine of revanche (revenge). **Hinge Question:** How did state-sponsored schoolroom indoctrination like that shown in Bettannier's painting ensure the hatred of Germany was passed down across generations?
source_context.Source E: Bismarck recognized that if France ever allied with Tsarist Russia, Germany would face the existential nightmare of a two-front war. To prevent this, he negotiated the ultra-secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887, guaranteeing Russian neutrality. When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890, he disastrously refused to renew this treaty. **Hinge Question:** Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II's abandonment of the Reinsurance Treaty in 1890 create the exact strategic catastrophe that Bismarck had spent twenty years preventing?

teacher_notes.curriculum_link: KS3 National Curriculum (Challenges 1901–Present): Pre-1914 European geopolitics — German unification (1871), Alsace-Lorraine, French revanche, and Bismarckian alliance diplomacy (Multi-Causal Explanation).
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why did annexing Alsace-Lorraine in May 1871 prove far more dangerous to long-term European peace than forcing France to pay 5 billion gold francs?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Strong answers explain that France paid off the 5 billion franc indemnity within a few years, whereas tearing away iron-and-coal-rich Alsace-Lorraine created a permanent open wound in French national identity ('revanche', seen in Bettannier's 1887 classroom painting Source D). That permanent hostility meant France could never reconcile with Berlin, locking Bismarck into constant dread of a two-front war with France and Russia. Probe any pupil who thinks Bismarck wanted endless expansion after 1871—point them to the 1887 Reinsurance Treaty (Source E) showing his defensive obsession with keeping Russia neutral.

misconceptions.misconception: Pupils often assume Germany had always existed as a single united country throughout modern European history.
misconceptions.correction: Before January 1871, Central Europe was divided into 39 separate German kingdoms, duchies, and free cities; Prussian Minister-President Otto von Bismarck united them through three wars against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866), and France (1870–71).

misconceptions.misconception: Pupils confuse the 1871 proclamation at Versailles with the 1919 Treaty of Versailles at the end of the First World War.
misconceptions.correction: Use Source B (Werner's painting) to anchor the chronology: Bismarck crowned Kaiser Wilhelm I inside Versailles's Hall of Mirrors in January 1871 to humiliate France—the exact reason French Premier Clemenceau chose the same hall to punish Germany in 1919.

misconceptions.misconception: Pupils assume Otto von Bismarck remained eager for further European conquests after 1871.
misconceptions.correction: Once Germany was unified in 1871, Bismarck viewed it as a 'satisfied power' and spent nineteen years weaving defensive treaties like the secret 1887 Reinsurance Treaty with Russia (Source E) to keep France isolated.

teacher_notes.send_adaptation: Pair the Block 4 Reference Map with Source D (La Tache Noire, showing Alsace-Lorraine shaded black on a French school map) and use the Block 5 profile deck plus the Recto PEEL sentence prompts to scaffold two clear causal paragraphs.
teacher_notes.stretch_challenge: Using Article I of the 1887 Reinsurance Treaty (Source E), explain why Bismarck's entire European peace system depended on a fragile personal balancing act between rival Austria-Hungary and Tsarist Russia.

items.question: What diplomatic term describes an international system where power is balanced among rival states so no single country dominates Europe?
items.explanation: For decades after 1815, European diplomacy aimed to preserve a stable Balance of Power among the Great Powers.

items.question: Which great economic transformation of the 18th and 19th centuries replaced hand workshops with steam engines, railways, and steel mills?
items.explanation: Industrialisation enabled nineteenth-century European powers to mass-produce rifles, artillery, railways, and iron warships.

items.question: How did the spread of steam railways change European warfare in the nineteenth century?
items.answer: Armies, weapons, and supplies could be moved rapidly to borders by train
items.explanation: Railways allowed generals to mobilise hundreds of thousands of troops to national frontiers in days instead of weeks.

items.question: Which two raw materials were most vital for powering nineteenth-century steam engines, railways, and steel armaments?
items.explanation: Control of coal mines and iron-ore fields directly determined a nation's industrial and military strength.

items.question: Why did Great Britain rely primarily on the Royal Navy rather than a massive conscript army in the nineteenth century?
items.answer: Britain is an island dependent on sea trade and imported food
items.explanation: Command of the seas protected Britain's coastline from invasion and safeguarded merchant shipping lanes.

items.question: What does the historical concept of "imperialism" mean?
items.answer: Building an empire by conquering and ruling overseas territories and peoples
items.explanation: European industrial powers competed across Africa and Asia for colonies, raw materials, ports, and prestige.

items.question: Which vast empire ruled by an autocratic Tsar stretched across Eastern Europe and northern Asia?
items.explanation: Tsarist Russia possessed Europe's largest population and army, bordering Eastern and Central Europe.

items.question: Which French Emperor had conquered much of Europe before his final defeat at Waterloo in 1815?
items.explanation: Memories of the Napoleonic Wars shaped European borders and diplomacy throughout the nineteenth century.

items.question: Which narrow stretch of sea separates southern Britain from France and Belgium?
items.explanation: Ensuring hostile powers never controlled the ports along the English Channel was a core British security priority.

items.question: Which sea lies between the eastern coast of Great Britain and the northern coastline of mainland Europe?
items.explanation: Naval rivalry in the North Sea directly threatened Britain's eastern ports and shipping routes.

items.question: What does military "conscription" require of young male citizens?
items.answer: Compulsory military training and service in the armed forces by law
items.explanation: Most continental European powers trained millions of reservists through peacetime conscription.

items.question: What is a "defensive alliance" between two or more nations?
items.answer: A formal treaty promising mutual military help if an ally is attacked
items.explanation: While intended to deter enemies, interlocking alliances risked turning a regional dispute into a continental war.

vocab.definition: Ruthless, practical statecraft based on national self-interest, industrial power, and military force rather than moral ideals.
The deep-seated French national desire for vengeance against Germany and the recovery of Alsace-Lorraine following the 1871 defeat.
The Prussian-led customs union formed in 1834 that created economic unity among German states while excluding Austria.
Mineral-rich French border provinces containing major iron-ore deposits and textile industries annexed by Germany in 1871.
A secret 1887 defensive agreement between Germany and Russia pledging benevolent neutrality if either faced war, preventing encirclement.

narrative_blocks.title: The Fragmented Chessboard, Zollverein & Prussian Power (1862–1866)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.1] In the mid-nineteenth century, Central Europe was fragmented into 39 separate German states divided between Austrian and Prussian influence. Determined to unite Germany under the Prussian monarchy, Minister-President Otto von Bismarck delivered his famous Bismarck’s Blood & Iron speech in 1862, arguing that military strength alone determined history.

Bismarck expanded Prussian armed forces through modern railways and lethal, breech-loading deadly Krupp steel guns. Prussian military technology outgunned Austria and Denmark, establishing Prussia as the unchallenged master of Northern Germany.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: 1870 Scientific American steel engraving depicting Krupp’s giant 50-ton breech-loading rifled cast-steel gun mounted on a heavy iron carriage with three pointed steel shells in the foreground and Prussian officers standing beside it
narrative_blocks.caption: Prussian Industrial Firepower — Krupp Breech-Loading Cast-Steel Cannon (Scientific American, 1870): Forged at Essen in the Ruhr, Krupp steel artillery and rapid railway mobilisation powered Bismarck’s "Blood and Iron" victories over Denmark (1864) and Austria (1866).

[1.1] In the mid-nineteenth century, Central Europe was fragmented into 39 separate German states divided between Austrian and Prussian influence. Determined to unite Germany under the Prussian monarchy, Minister-President Otto von Bismarck delivered his famous Bismarck’s Blood & Iron speech in 1862, arguing that military strength alone determined history.

narrative_blocks.title: The Sedan Debacle & Proclamation at Versailles (1870–1871)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.2] In July 1870, Bismarck provoked war with France to rally the independent southern German kingdoms into a national union. At the Battle of Sedan, Prussian encirclement resulted in French Emperor captured at Sedan alongside eighty thousand soldiers, toppling Emperor Napoleon III’s imperial regime.

On 18 January 1871, German princes gathered in the Palace of Versailles where the German Empire crowned at Versailles, appointing Kaiser Wilhelm I. Following victory, Prussia dominates Europe as the continent’s leading industrial and military titan.

source.model_answer: Bismarck staged the proclamation in the Hall of Mirrors to inflict maximum psychological and symbolic humiliation on defeated France, visibly demonstrating that German military supremacy had superseded historic French dominance in Europe.

narrative_blocks.content:
[1.2] In July 1870, Bismarck provoked war with France to rally the independent southern German kingdoms into a national union. At the Battle of Sedan, Prussian encirclement resulted in French Emperor captured at Sedan alongside eighty thousand soldiers, toppling Emperor Napoleon III’s imperial regime.

On 18 January 1871, German princes gathered in the Palace of Versailles where the German Empire crowned at Versailles, appointing Kaiser Wilhelm I. Following victory, Prussia dominates Europe as the continent’s leading industrial and military titan.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Historical painting by Wilhelm Camphausen (1878) showing captured French Emperor Napoleon III in blue greatcoat and red trousers seated gloomily outside a weaver’s cottage at Donchery beside Prussian Chancellor Otto von Bismarck in spiked helmet and riding boots on 2 September 1870
narrative_blocks.caption: Napoleon III Captured After Sedan (2 September 1870, painting by Wilhelm Camphausen, 1878, Deutsches Historisches Museum): Following Prussian encirclement at Sedan, Bismarck met the defeated French Emperor before crowning Wilhelm I as German Kaiser at Versailles.

narrative_blocks.title: The Treaty of Frankfurt & Annexation of Alsace-Lorraine (May 1871)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.3] The 1871 Treaty of Frankfurt imposed harsh punitive terms on defeated France. Bismarck ordered German occupation troops to remain in French cities until the French forced to pay 5 billion gold francs in war indemnities.

Crucially, France was humiliated by losing coal and iron land through the annexation of the wealthy border provinces of Alsace-Lorraine. This painful territorial seizure created enduring hatred between France and Germany that poisoned European international relations for four decades.

source.title: Source C (State Treaty): The Treaty of Frankfurt, Articles I & VII (10 May 1871)
source.text:
Article I: The French Republic cedes to His Majesty the Emperor of Germany all sovereign rights and titles over the territories situated east of the frontier specified hereafter: the provinces of Upper and Lower Alsace... and the eastern districts of Lorraine including the fortress city of Metz.

Article VII: The payment of the war indemnity of five thousand million francs (5,000,000,000 francs) shall take place within three years. German occupation troops shall evacuate French departments sequentially only as each instalment is paid in gold coin.
source.caption: Official diplomatic text of the Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871), imposing severe territorial annexations and financial penalties on the defeated French Third Republic.
source.citation: French Diplomatic Archives, La Courneuve / Reichsgesetzblatt 1871, No. 23.
source.context: Under the Treaty of Frankfurt, Germany annexed the mineral-rich provinces of Alsace and eastern Lorraine without a plebiscite and forced France to pay a staggering 5 billion gold franc indemnity. This treaty created a permanent grievance in French political life.
source.question: What does the severe language of the Treaty of Frankfurt reveal about Bismarck's strategic intentions towards France?
source.model_answer: The treaty reveals Bismarck's intention to cripple France economically with a colossal five billion franc indemnity and strip away its strategic frontier fortresses, attempting to prevent France from recovering quickly enough to challenge Germany.

narrative_blocks.title: French Revanche & The Cult of the Lost Provinces (1871–1889)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.4] Across the French Third Republic, the loss of Alsace-Lorraine inspired revanche—a national desire for vengeance against Germany. In primary schools across the nation, patriotic teachers kept classroom maps veiled in black crepe paper to mourn the lost eastern provinces every morning.

French schoolchildren grew up dreaming of French revenge and the future liberation of their homeland. The French government introduced universal army conscription for boys reaching twenty, training millions of young citizens for an unavoidable continental war.

narrative_blocks.caption: Reference Map: German Unification (1871), the seizure of Alsace-Lorraine under the Treaty of Frankfurt, French Revanche, and Chancellor Bismarck’s diplomatic web to prevent a two-front war (1871–1890).

source.caption: Albert Bettannier's 1887 painting showing a French schoolmaster pointing out the blacked-out provinces of Alsace-Lorraine to young schoolboys wearing military-style cadet uniforms.
source.citation: Musée de la Cour d'Or, Metz (Inv. Bettannier-1887-Metz).
source.context: Following 1871, the French Third Republic mobilized the state education system to keep the memory of the 'lost provinces' alive. Schoolboys were instructed in military drill, gymnastics, and patriotic history under the doctrine of revanche (revenge).
source.question: What message was Albert Bettannier communicating about French national identity and schooling in the late nineteenth century?
source.model_answer: Bettannier was highlighting how French schools deliberately educated boys from childhood to view the recovery of Alsace-Lorraine as an sacred national duty, preparing the next generation for future war against Germany.

narrative_blocks.title: Bismarckian Isolation, The Reinsurance Treaty & Two-Front Dread (1871–1890)
narrative_blocks.text:
[1.5] As Imperial Chancellor, Otto von Bismarck devoted his diplomatic career to keeping France isolated from potential European allies. Bismarck was permanently haunted by the existential fear of war on two fronts against France in the west and Tsarist Russia in the east.

To safeguard Germany’s eastern frontier, Bismarck negotiated a secret deal with Russia in the 1887 Reinsurance Treaty, promising mutual neutrality. Through cautious diplomacy, Bismarck balanced European alliances and protected the newly created German Reich.

source.title: Source E (Secret Treaty): The Reinsurance Treaty Between Germany and Russia (18 June 1887)
source.text:
Article I: In case one of the High Contracting Parties should find itself at war with a third Great Power, the other would maintain a benevolent neutrality toward it, and would devote its efforts to the localization of the conflict. This provision would not apply to a war against Austria or France in case this war should result from an attack directed against one of these two latter Powers by one of the High Contracting Parties.

Article II: Germany recognizes the legitimacy of the decisive influence which Russia exercises in Bulgaria... Both courts pledge to take diplomatic steps to prevent any alteration of the territorial status quo on the Balkan Peninsula.
source.caption: Confidential treaty negotiated secretly by Bismarck in Berlin, binding Germany and the Russian Empire in mutual benevolent neutrality.
source.citation: Political Archive of the German Foreign Office, Berlin (PA AA, Geheimverträge 1887).
source.context: Bismarck recognized that if France ever allied with Tsarist Russia, Germany would face the existential nightmare of a two-front war. To prevent this, he negotiated the ultra-secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887, guaranteeing Russian neutrality. When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890, he disastrously refused to renew this treaty.
source.question: How does the Reinsurance Treaty demonstrate Bismarck's obsession with avoiding a two-front war against France and Russia?
source.model_answer: The treaty shows Bismarck was willing to grant Russia secret diplomatic concessions in the Balkans in order to secure Russian neutrality, ensuring France could never form an alliance that would trap Germany between two hostile fronts.

tasks.model_answer:
A primary reason the creation of the German Empire in 1871 created long-term instability was that it radically altered the European balance of power. After defeating France, unified Germany became the dominant military and industrial superpower in central Europe. To prevent French revenge for the loss of Alsace-Lorraine, Chancellor Otto von Bismarck created complex alliances that divided Europe into competing camps.

Furthermore, Kaiser Wilhelm II’s aggressive foreign policy ('Weltpolitik') after 1890 increased friction. Demanding Germany's 'place in the sun', the Kaiser challenged British naval supremacy and meddled in colonial disputes, triggering a dangerous atmosphere of suspicion.

sources.title: Source C (State Treaty): The Treaty of Frankfurt, Articles I & VII (10 May 1871)
sources.text:
Article I: The French Republic cedes to His Majesty the Emperor of Germany all sovereign rights and titles over the territories situated east of the frontier specified hereafter: the provinces of Upper and Lower Alsace... and the eastern districts of Lorraine including the fortress city of Metz.

Article VII: The payment of the war indemnity of five thousand million francs (5,000,000,000 francs) shall take place within three years. German occupation troops shall evacuate French departments sequentially only as each instalment is paid in gold coin.
sources.caption: Official diplomatic text of the Treaty of Frankfurt (10 May 1871), imposing severe territorial annexations and financial penalties on the defeated French Third Republic.
sources.citation: French Diplomatic Archives, La Courneuve / Reichsgesetzblatt 1871, No. 23.
sources.context: Under the Treaty of Frankfurt, Germany annexed the mineral-rich provinces of Alsace and eastern Lorraine without a plebiscite and forced France to pay a staggering 5 billion gold franc indemnity. This treaty created a permanent grievance in French political life.
sources.question: What does the severe language of the Treaty of Frankfurt reveal about Bismarck's strategic intentions towards France?
sources.model_answer: The treaty reveals Bismarck's intention to cripple France economically with a colossal five billion franc indemnity and strip away its strategic frontier fortresses, attempting to prevent France from recovering quickly enough to challenge Germany.
sources.source_context: Under the Treaty of Frankfurt, Germany annexed the mineral-rich provinces of Alsace and eastern Lorraine without a plebiscite and forced France to pay a staggering 5 billion gold franc indemnity. This treaty created a permanent grievance in French political life.

sources.context: Following 1871, the French Third Republic mobilized the state education system to keep the memory of the 'lost provinces' alive. Schoolboys were instructed in military drill, gymnastics, and patriotic history under the doctrine of revanche (revenge).

sources.model_answer: Bettannier was highlighting how French schools deliberately educated boys from childhood to view the recovery of Alsace-Lorraine as an sacred national duty, preparing the next generation for future war against Germany.

sources.title: Source E (Secret Treaty): The Reinsurance Treaty Between Germany and Russia (18 June 1887)
sources.text:
Article I: In case one of the High Contracting Parties should find itself at war with a third Great Power, the other would maintain a benevolent neutrality toward it, and would devote its efforts to the localization of the conflict. This provision would not apply to a war against Austria or France in case this war should result from an attack directed against one of these two latter Powers by one of the High Contracting Parties.

Article II: Germany recognizes the legitimacy of the decisive influence which Russia exercises in Bulgaria... Both courts pledge to take diplomatic steps to prevent any alteration of the territorial status quo on the Balkan Peninsula.
sources.caption: Confidential treaty negotiated secretly by Bismarck in Berlin, binding Germany and the Russian Empire in mutual benevolent neutrality.
sources.citation: Political Archive of the German Foreign Office, Berlin (PA AA, Geheimverträge 1887).
sources.context: Bismarck recognized that if France ever allied with Tsarist Russia, Germany would face the existential nightmare of a two-front war. To prevent this, he negotiated the ultra-secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887, guaranteeing Russian neutrality. When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890, he disastrously refused to renew this treaty.
sources.question: How does the Reinsurance Treaty demonstrate Bismarck's obsession with avoiding a two-front war against France and Russia?
sources.model_answer: The treaty shows Bismarck was willing to grant Russia secret diplomatic concessions in the Balkans in order to secure Russian neutrality, ensuring France could never form an alliance that would trap Germany between two hostile fronts.
sources.source_context: Bismarck recognized that if France ever allied with Tsarist Russia, Germany would face the existential nightmare of a two-front war. To prevent this, he negotiated the ultra-secret Reinsurance Treaty of 1887, guaranteeing Russian neutrality. When Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890, he disastrously refused to renew this treaty.

stages.connective: Alarmed Britain and France, who viewed German imperial ambition as a direct threat to their overseas colonies and trade.
stages.question: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II sack Bismarck and launch Weltpolitik in 1890?

stages.title: The First Moroccan Crisis (Tangier)
stages.trigger: Kaiser Wilhelm II lands at Tangier on a white horse, publicly backing Moroccan independence to challenge French colonial dominance.
stages.connective: Attempted to test and divide the 1904 Entente Cordiale, but instead brought the European powers to the brink of war.
stages.question: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II ride into Tangier on a white horse in 1905?

stages.title: The Algeciras Conference Humiliation
stages.trigger: At the conference in Spain, Britain, Russia, and Italy all vote to back French control in Morocco, leaving Germany isolated.
stages.connective: Deeply humiliated Germany and convinced Britain and France to begin secret joint military conversations for mutual defence.
stages.question: How did the 1906 Algeciras Conference backfire on German diplomacy?

stages.title: The Agadir Crisis (The Panther’s Leap)
stages.trigger: Germany sends the gunboat SMS Panther to Agadir, demanding the French Congo in exchange for accepting French control of Morocco.
stages.connective: Britain firmly backed France with the Mansion House speech; Germany backed down, feeling encircled and preparing for war.
stages.question: Why did sending the gunboat Panther to Agadir in 1911 alarm Britain?

video.title: What was the 'Scramble for Africa'? - BBC What's New

Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–02:45 • Lesson Phase: Quick Starter Check (0–3m). Tone Alert: Fast, accessible animated educational summary.
video.viewing_task:
1. [00:45] Quick Check: What percentage of the African continent was colonized by European imperial powers between 1881 and 1914 during the "Scramble for Africa"?
  2. [02:00] Hinge Question: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II's demand for Germany to have a "place in the sun" (Platz an der Sonne) alarm the established British and French global empires?
video.model_answer:
1. Quick Check: Approximately 90% of the continent (up from only 10% in 1870).
  2. Hinge Question: By the time Germany unified in 1871, Britain and France had already seized the most lucrative colonial territories, shipping routes, and mineral reserves. When Wilhelm II announced his aggressive policy of Weltpolitik (world policy) to build a global colonial empire, Germany could expand only by challenging British and French spheres of influence, directly creating colonial flashpoints like the Moroccan Crises.

video.title: The Scramble for Africa Explained: Imperialism, Empire, and the Road to World War I
video.teacher_guidance: Detailed analysis of the 1884 Berlin Conference convened by Bismarck, the First Moroccan Crisis (Tangier 1905), the Second Moroccan Crisis (Agadir 1911), and the consolidation of the Entente Cordiale. Recommended Watch Window: 01:15–07:45 • Lesson Phase: Guided Instruction & Archival Investigation. Tone Alert: Comprehensive, analytical imperial history.
video.viewing_task:
1. [02:15] Recall: Which German gunboat did Kaiser Wilhelm II dispatch to the Atlantic port of Agadir in July 1911 to challenge French colonial dominance in Morocco?
  2. [04:45] Explain: Explain the outcome of the 1906 Algeciras Conference: how did Germany's attempt to drive a wedge between Britain and France backfire catastrophically?
  3. [06:50] Challenge: Evaluate how imperial rivalry in Africa cemented the 1904 Anglo-French Entente Cordiale: why did colonial crises transform a colonial settlement into a de facto military alliance?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The gunboat SMS Panther (the "Panther's Spring").
  2. Explain: At Algeciras, only Austria-Hungary supported Germany, while Britain, Russia, Italy, and the United States backed France's special police mandate in Morocco. Germany suffered a humiliating diplomatic isolation, while Britain and France were drawn into secret naval and military staff conversations, strengthening the very Anglo-French alliance the Kaiser had sought to shatter.
  3. Challenge: The 1904 Entente Cordiale was initially merely an agreement resolving overseas colonial disputes (recognizing British control of Egypt and French influence in Morocco). However, German gunboat intimidation at Tangier and Agadir convinced British foreign policy leaders that Germany sought naval dominance on the Atlantic and hegemonial conquest of Europe, leading Britain to commit to defending French northern coastal waters.

video.title: Crisis in Morocco (1905 & 1911): How Imperial Rivalry Helped Start WW1
video.teacher_guidance: Focused breakdown of Kaiser Wilhelm II's 1905 Tangier speech, the Algeciras Conference, and the 1911 Agadir gunboat crisis (SMS Panther), demonstrating how German Weltpolitik backfired by driving Britain and France closer together. Recommended Watch Window: 00:00–05:02 • Lesson Phase: Core Case Study.
video.viewing_task:
1. [00:50] Recall: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II visit Tangier in 1905 and send the gunboat SMS Panther to Agadir in 1911?
  2. [02:30] Explain: Explain how Germany's attempt to split the 1904 Entente Cordiale between Britain and France completely backfired.
  3. [04:10] Challenge: Why did colonial clashes in North Africa make a European war more likely by 1914 even though neither Moroccan Crisis caused immediate war?
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: To challenge French expansion in Morocco, demand 'a place in the sun' for German Weltpolitik, and test whether Britain would stand by France.
  2. Explain: Instead of breaking the Entente Cordiale, German bullying alarmed London (especially Lloyd George's Mansion House speech in 1911) and led Britain and France into secret joint naval and military staff talks.
  3. Challenge: Each humiliation left Berlin feeling encircled and determined not to back down in the next diplomatic crisis, turning rival alliances into hair-trigger military blocs before July 1914.

video.title: Powder Keg: Europe 1900 to 1914 | Historical Documentary | Lucasfilm
video.teacher_guidance: Examines the global web of imperial competition, the tension between autocracy and democracy, and how colonial disputes hardened national rivalries into armed camps. Recommended Watch Window: 02:00–08:30 • Lesson Phase: Guided Instruction & Synoptic Evaluation. Tone Alert: High-production archival documentary featuring primary footage and scholar commentary.
video.viewing_task:
1. [03:30] Recall: What crucial waterway connecting the Mediterranean to the Red Sea did Great Britain regard as the indispensable imperial lifeline to British India?
  2. [05:45] Explain: How did social Darwinist theories and competitive imperial nationalism convince European publics and military leaders that war was a natural, purifying test of national vitality?
  3. [07:50] Challenge: Evaluate whether imperial competition in Africa and Asia was a primary cause of World War I or merely a symptom of European national rivalries.
video.model_answer:
1. Recall: The Suez Canal (opened in 1869).
  2. Explain: Pervasive imperial propaganda and pseudoscience argued that nations, like biological species, were engaged in a struggle for "survival of the fittest." Newspapers and school textbooks glorified military conquest and imperial expansion, cultivating an arrogant bellicosity where compromise was viewed as national weakness and decadence.
  3. Challenge: While colonial crises (such as Fashoda, Tangier, and Agadir) nearly sparked war, European powers repeatedly resolved them through negotiated territorial trade-offs. The crucial danger of imperialism was indirect: it fueled the naval arms race, deepened psychological paranoia, and solidified the Anglo-French-Russian alliance system that made a localized Balkan conflict uncontrollable.

lessons.skill: Causation & Imperial Rivalry: The Scramble for Africa & Morocco
lessons.title: Enquiry 2: Imperial Rivalry, the Scramble for Africa & the Moroccan Crises (1884–1911)
lessons.subtitle: From the Berlin Conference and Weltpolitik to the Brink of War at Tangier and Agadir
lessons.enquiryQuestion: How did colonial rivalry in Africa and Kaiser Wilhelm’s ambitions fuel tension?

teacher_notes.primer: This enquiry explores how imperial competition outside Europe poisoned relations between the Great Powers. In 1884, Bismarck convened the Berlin Conference to peacefully divide Africa under the doctrine of "effective occupation." But when Kaiser Wilhelm II dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and launched "Weltpolitik" demanding Germany’s "place in the sun," imperial expansion became aggressive and confrontational. The lesson focuses on the First Moroccan Crisis (1905, Tangier) and Second Moroccan Crisis (1911, Agadir), demonstrating how German attempts to fracture the Anglo-French Entente Cordiale completely backfired, driving Britain and France into secret joint military and naval planning.

objectives.objective: Explain why European powers partitioned Africa at the 1884–85 Berlin Conference.
objectives.primer: Focus on paragraph [2.1]. Emphasize the search for raw materials (rubber, minerals, cotton) and national prestige, regulated by Bismarck’s doctrine of effective occupation.
objectives.question: Why did European empires prefer to establish rules at Berlin rather than fight wars directly over African territory?

objectives.objective: Analyze how Kaiser Wilhelm II’s policy of "Weltpolitik" altered German foreign policy.
objectives.primer: Direct students to paragraph [2.2]. Compare Bismarck’s cautious European balance of power with Wilhelm II’s bellicose demand for a global colonial empire.
objectives.question: What did Wilhelm II mean by demanding Germany’s "place in the sun", and why did this alarm Great Britain?

objectives.objective: Evaluate how the Moroccan Crises cemented the Anglo-French Entente and isolated Germany.
objectives.primer: Focus on paragraphs [2.3] to [2.5]. Show how the Kaiser’s landing at Tangier and the dispatch of the gunboat Panther to Agadir united Britain and France against Germany.
objectives.question: Why did Germany’s aggressive "gunboat diplomacy" in Morocco achieve the exact opposite of what Berlin intended?

source_context.Source A: At the 1884–1885 Berlin Conference, Chancellor Bismarck orchestrated the formal partition of Africa, acquiring Germany's first official protectorates in South-West Africa (Angra Pequena/Namibia), Togoland, Cameroon, and German New Guinea. British public opinion was startled by Germany's sudden entry into colonial expansion, portraying Bismarck as a greedy table-companion taking colonial territories Britain considered its natural sphere of influence. **Hinge Question:** How does Tenniel's depiction of Bismarck taking 'Angra Pequena' reveal Britain's resentment when other European powers claimed colonial territory?
source_context.Source B: In 1897, the German government abandoned Bismarck's cautious continental diplomacy in favour of Weltpolitik (world policy), demanding global colonies and prestige equivalent to Britain's. **Hinge Question:** How did the rhetoric of demanding a 'place in the sun' convince other European powers that Germany was no longer a satisfied power, but an aggressive challenger?
source_context.Source C: By the late 19th century, Great Britain governed an empire covering approximately a quarter of the globe and one-fifth of the world's population. When Kaiser Wilhelm II and Chancellor Bülow demanded Germany's 'place in the sun' in the late 1890s, they looked with intense envy at British global dominance illustrated in imperial maps like Crane's, feeling that Germany was confined to Central Europe while Britain monopolized global commerce and colonies. **Hinge Question:** Why did the overwhelming visual reality of the British Empire across the globe make German leaders believe that peaceful commercial expansion was impossible without challenging British hegemony?
source_context.Source D: In 1905, Germany provoked the First Moroccan Crisis by landing Kaiser Wilhelm II at Tangier to champion Moroccan independence against French colonial claims. Germany hoped to expose the 1904 Entente Cordiale as weak; instead, the crisis backfired and drew Britain and France closer together. **Hinge Question:** Why did the Kaiser's dramatic intervention at Tangier ultimately strengthen Anglo-French military cooperation instead of fracturing it?
source_context.Source E: During the Second Moroccan Crisis (1911), Chancellor David Lloyd George—previously regarded as a pacifist-leaning Radical—delivered a blistering public warning that Britain would fight rather than allow Germany to bully France or threaten maritime routes. **Hinge Question:** Why was Lloyd George's Mansion House speech a decisive psychological turning point in the road to the Great War?

teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II's theatrical interventions in Morocco at Tangier (1905) and Agadir (1911) achieve the exact opposite of what Berlin intended?
teacher_notes.hinge_guidance: Look for pupils identifying Berlin's goal—humiliating France and shattering the young 1904 Anglo-French Entente Cordiale—and contrasting it with the real outcome: twelve-to-two isolation at the 1906 Algeciras Conference, secret Anglo-French joint military staff talks, and Lloyd George's stern July 1911 Mansion House warning (Source E). misconceptions.misconception: Pupils assume European powers fought battles against one another inside Africa during the 1884–85 Berlin Conference.
misconceptions.correction: Bismarck convened the Berlin Conference precisely to avoid intra-European war while partitioning African land under 'effective occupation' rules, without inviting a single African leader to the table.

misconceptions.misconception: Pupils confuse Bismarck's cautious European diplomacy with Kaiser Wilhelm II's aggressive global Weltpolitik.
misconceptions.correction: Wilhelm II forced Bismarck's resignation in 1890 specifically to abandon quiet continental treaties and pursue overseas colonies and naval prestige—demanding Germany's 'place in the sun' (Source B).

misconceptions.misconception: Pupils think the 1904 Entente Cordiale was already a binding military alliance obliging Britain to fight for France.
misconceptions.correction: In 1904 the Entente Cordiale merely settled colonial disputes in Egypt and Morocco; it was Germany's own gunboat bullying at Tangier (1905) and Agadir (1911) that drove London and Paris into secret joint military and naval planning.

items.question: Which state was the most powerful among the German states before 1871?

items.question: What was Bismarck's famous phrase for how Germany would be unified?

items.question: Who became the Prime Minister of Prussia in 1862?
items.explanation: As Imperial Chancellor, Otto von Bismarck devoted his diplomatic career to keeping France isolated from potential European allies.

items.question: What did Bismarck declare would decide the great questions of the day instead of speeches and votes?
items.explanation: Determined to unite Germany under the Prussian monarchy, Minister-President Otto von Bismarck delivered his famous Bismarck’s Blood & Iron speech in 1862, arguing that military strength alone determined history.

items.question: In what year did the Franco-Prussian War begin?
items.explanation: In July 1870, Bismarck provoked war with France to rally the independent southern German kingdoms into a national union.

items.question: Which valuable French territory did Germany seize in 1871?
items.explanation: Crucially, France was humiliated by losing coal and iron land through the annexation of the wealthy border provinces of Alsace-Lorraine.

items.explanation: Across the French Third Republic, losing Alsace-Lorraine fuelled revanche — a lasting national longing to reclaim the lost provinces.

items.question: What strategic nightmare haunted Chancellor Otto von Bismarck throughout his diplomatic career after 1871?
items.answer: War on two fronts against France and Russia
items.explanation: Situated in Central Europe, Bismarck feared fighting simultaneous war on two fronts against France in the west and Russia in the east.

vocab.definition: Kaiser Wilhelm II’s aggressive "World Policy" aiming to transform Germany into a global superpower with overseas colonies and a battlefleet.
The pursuit of foreign policy objectives through conspicuous displays of naval military force to intimidate rivals.
The 1904 diplomatic agreement between Great Britain and France resolving colonial disputes and inaugurating diplomatic cooperation.
The 1906 international summit where twelve nations backed France in Morocco, leaving Germany diplomatically isolated.
A 1911 public speech by British Chancellor David Lloyd George warning Germany that Britain would not allow France to be bullied.

narrative_blocks.title: The Scramble for Africa & The Berlin Conference (1884–1885)
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.1] In the late nineteenth century, European empires engaged in carving up African land during the competitive Scramble for Africa. Industrial powers sought overseas colonies to exploit raw materials, including valuable rubber, copper & mineral riches, palm oil, and cotton.

To prevent armed clashes among rival powers, Chancellor Bismarck organized the 1884 Berlin Conference. The rules made at Berlin meeting established that empires had to prove "effective occupation", prompting a rapid rush to conquer the African interior.

stage_hook_map.title: Scramble for Africa & The Moroccan Crises (1884–1911)
stage_hook_map.subtitle: Berlin Conference, Tangier, Algeciras, Agadir & Weltpolitik · Tap numbered pins 1–5

pins.label: 1. Berlin Conference (1884–85)
pins.title: Berlin Conference Verdict (1884–85): Carving Up Africa on Paper
pins.body: Hosted by Chancellor Bismarck in Berlin without inviting a single African ruler, fourteen Western powers agreed the rule of “effective occupation” to claim African land. Within twenty years, European empires carved up roughly 90% of Africa for rubber, copper, gold, diamonds, and imperial prestige—leaving only Abyssinia and Liberia independent.

Within twenty years, European empires carved up roughly 90% of Africa for rubber, copper, gold, diamonds, and imperial prestige—leaving only Abyssinia and Liberia independent.
pins.hinge: Why did the Berlin Conference’s “effective occupation” rule speed up armed European conquest across the African interior?

pins.label: 2. Tangier Crisis (Mar 1905)
pins.title: Tangier, Morocco (March 1905): Kaiser Wilhelm II Tests the Entente
pins.body: In March 1905, Kaiser Wilhelm II landed dramatically at Tangier and rode a white horse through the streets declaring support for an independent Moroccan Sultan. Wilhelm aimed to block French control of Morocco and shatter the brand-new 1904 Anglo-French Entente Cordiale—but his gamble backfired.

pins.hinge: Why did Kaiser Wilhelm II deliberately provoke a crisis in Tangier less than a year after Britain and France signed the 1904 Entente Cordiale?

pins.label: 3. Algeciras Summit (1906)
pins.title: Algeciras Conference, Spain (1906): German Diplomatic Isolation
pins.body: At the international conference in Algeciras across the bay from British Gibraltar, Germany was humiliatingly outvoted 12 nations to 2—supported only by Austria-Hungary. Far from splitting the Entente, German bullying drove Britain and France to begin secret joint military staff talks.

pins.hinge: How did the 1906 Algeciras vote achieve the exact opposite of what Kaiser Wilhelm II had hoped for in Tangier?

pins.label: 4. Agadir Gunboat (Jul 1911)
pins.title: Agadir, Morocco (July 1911): Gunboat SMS Panther & Mansion House Warning
pins.body: When French troops entered Fez in 1911, Germany sent the gunboat SMS Panther to the Atlantic port of Agadir. Alarmed that Germany wanted an Atlantic naval base near Gibraltar sea lanes, British Chancellor David Lloyd George issued his Mansion House warning that Britain would fight rather than see France bullied—forcing Germany to back down.

pins.hinge: Why did a German gunboat anchoring at Agadir on Morocco’s Atlantic coast alarm Great Britain even more than France?

pins.label: 5. German Colonies (Weltpolitik)
pins.title: German Colonies (“A Place in the Sun”): Weltpolitik & Naval Rivalry
pins.body: Dismissing Bismarck in 1890, Kaiser Wilhelm II launched Weltpolitik (“World Policy”) to win Germany “a place in the sun.” Ruling Togoland, Kamerun, German South-West Africa, and German East Africa convinced Berlin it needed a massive Dreadnought battle fleet—triggering a bitter naval arms race with Britain.

narrative_blocks.title: Kaiser Wilhelm II,"Weltpolitik" & "A Place in the Sun" (1890–1897)
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.2] In 1890, twenty-nine-year-old Kaiser Wilhelm II forced the sudden resignation of the veteran Chancellor. Kaiser sacks old Bismarck to abandon cautious European balance-of-power treaties in favour of an aggressive global strategy known as Weltpolitik ("World Policy").

Wilhelm envied the vast overseas territories of Great Britain and France, loudly demanding a place in the sun for the German nation. Building a German empire across Africa, Asia, and the Pacific required colonial acquisitions and a battle fleet to challenge British naval mastery.

source.title: Source B (Parliamentary Speech): Bernhard von Bülow, Speech on Germany's "Place in the Sun" (1897)
source.text: The days when Germans abandoned the land to one neighbor and the sea to another, reserving for themselves only the heavens where pure doctrine reigns—those days are over! We do not want to put anyone into the shade, but we too demand our place in the sun (*einen Platz an der Sonne*). In East Asia and Africa, we cannot and will not allow any foreign power to push us aside or monopolize economic trade.
source.caption: Speech delivered by German Foreign Secretary (later Chancellor) Bernhard von Bülow to the Reichstag in Berlin, inaugurating Germany's aggressive global foreign policy (*Weltpolitik*).
source.citation: Stenographische Berichte über die Verhandlungen des Deutschen Reichstages, 1897, Vol. 1, p. 60.
source.context: In 1897, the German government abandoned Bismarck's cautious continental diplomacy in favour of Weltpolitik (world policy), demanding global colonies and prestige equivalent to Britain's.
source.question: Why did Bernhard von Bülow deliver this speech to the German Reichstag in December 1897?
source.model_answer: Bülow delivered the speech to rally parliamentary and public support for expanding Germany's colonial empire and navy, declaring that Germany would aggressively challenge existing British and French dominance to secure global prestige.

narrative_blocks.title: The First Moroccan Crisis & The Landing at Tangier (March 1905)
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.3] In March 1905, Kaiser Wilhelm challenged expanding French influence across North Africa by landing unannounced at Tangier. In a theatrical show of imperial defiance, the Kaiser rides white horse through the streets to the German embassy.

Wilhelm was actively testing Britain and France following their 1904 Entente Cordiale agreement, openly promising to protect Morocco as a free, independent sovereign state. Wilhelm intended to humiliate the French Republic and split the fledgling Anglo-French alliance before European eyes.

source.caption: Walter Crane's iconic 1886 map for The Graphic, illustrating the vast global expanse of the British Empire (shaded in red), Britannia seated on the globe, and imperial statistics compiled by Captain J.C.R. Colomb.
source.citation: The Graphic, London (24 July 1886) / Norman B. Leventhal Map Center, Boston Public Library (Call No. G3201.F7 1886 .C7).
source.context: By the late 19th century, Great Britain governed an empire covering approximately a quarter of the globe and one-fifth of the world's population. When Kaiser Wilhelm II and Chancellor Bülow demanded Germany's 'place in the sun' in the late 1890s, they looked with intense envy at British global dominance illustrated in imperial maps like Crane's, feeling that Germany was confined to Central Europe while Britain monopolized global commerce and colonies.

narrative_blocks.image_alt: Contemporary March 1905 press photograph showing Kaiser Wilhelm II in spiked helmet riding a white horse through the crowded, flag-draped streets of Tangier surrounded by Moroccan guards and onlookers
narrative_blocks.caption: The First Moroccan Crisis — Kaiser Wilhelm II Rides Through Tangier (31 March 1905): Disembarking from his steamer to ride a white horse to the German legation, Wilhelm loudly backed Moroccan independence to test the new 1904 Anglo-French Entente Cordiale.

narrative_blocks.title: The Algeciras Conference & German Diplomatic Isolation (1906)
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.4] The Moroccan dispute was settled at the 1906 Algeciras Conference in Spain. The international summit proved a catastrophic diplomatic setback for Berlin: Germany defeated in vote by twelve nations to two, with only Austria-Hungary supporting the German delegation.

Throughout the crisis, Britain backs up France completely, initiating secret joint military staff conversations in London. Instead of breaking the Entente, German bullying cemented Anglo-French defense ties, leaving German leaders fearing being surrounded by hostile powers on all borders.
narrative_blocks.image_alt: Bernard Partridge cartoon for Punch showing John Bull and French Marianne walking arm-in-arm down the street while Kaiser Wilhelm II stands stiffly in German military greatcoat pretending not to notice
narrative_blocks.caption: Anglo-French Solidarity Against German Pressure (Bernard Partridge, Punch): Instead of splitting Britain and France at the 1906 Algeciras Conference, Wilhelm’s Moroccan bullying turned the 1904 Entente Cordiale into close diplomatic and military cooperation.

source.title: Source D (Imperial Telegram): Kaiser Wilhelm II, Telegram from Tangier to Chancellor Bülow (1905)
source.text: Today I visited the Sultan's representative in Tangier and announced in person that I regard the Sultan of Morocco as an absolutely free and independent sovereign, subject to no foreign control. I declared that Germany insists upon equal commercial rights for all nations, and will never suffer any other power [France] to establish an exclusive protectorate here without international consent.
source.caption: Kaiser Wilhelm II's official dispatch describing his provocative visit to Tangier, Morocco, designed to test and break the newly signed 1904 Anglo-French Entente Cordiale.
source.citation: Die Große Politik der Europäischen Kabinette 1871–1914, Vol. 20, Part 2, Document 6589.
source.context: In 1905, Germany provoked the First Moroccan Crisis by landing Kaiser Wilhelm II at Tangier to champion Moroccan independence against French colonial claims. Germany hoped to expose the 1904 Entente Cordiale as weak; instead, the crisis backfired and drew Britain and France closer together.
source.question: What does this dispatch reveal about Kaiser Wilhelm II's underlying strategy during the First Moroccan Crisis?
source.model_answer: The dispatch reveals that the Kaiser used the pretence of Moroccan independence to directly challenge French colonial expansion, aiming to humiliate France and test whether Britain would honour its diplomatic support.

narrative_blocks.title: The Second Moroccan Crisis: The Panther at Agadir & Mansion House (July 1911)
narrative_blocks.text:
[2.5] In July 1911, imperial tensions erupted again when French forces marched to suppress unrest in Fez. Germany reacted aggressively: the gunboat sent to bully France, SMS Panther, anchored threateningly inside the Moroccan port of Agadir.

British leaders feared Germany sought an Atlantic naval base. In his famous Mansion House speech, Chancellor David Lloyd George issues warning that Britain would fight to defend international standing. Humiliated into retreat, Germany watched Britain and France plan for war with coordinated naval deployments.

source.title: Source E (Ministerial Speech): David Lloyd George, The Mansion House Speech (21 July 1911)
source.text: I am also bound to say this: that I believe it is essential in the highest interests, not merely of this country, but of the world, that Britain should at all hazards maintain her place and her prestige amongst the Great Powers of the world... If a situation were to be forced upon us in which peace could only be preserved by the surrender of the great and beneficent position Britain has won with centuries of heroism and achievement, by allowing Britain to be treated where her interests were vitally affected as if she didn't count in the Cabinet of Nations, then I say emphatically that peace at that price would be a humiliation intolerable for a great country like ours to endure.
source.caption: David Lloyd George addressing the annual Bankers' Dinner at Mansion House, delivering an unambiguous public warning to Germany following the dispatch of the gunboat Panther to Agadir.
source.citation: The Times (London), 22 July 1911, p. 7; Hansard Parliamentary Debates.
source.context: During the Second Moroccan Crisis (1911), Chancellor David Lloyd George—previously regarded as a pacifist-leaning Radical—delivered a blistering public warning that Britain would fight rather than allow Germany to bully France or threaten maritime routes.
source.question: What makes Lloyd George's Mansion House speech particularly significant as evidence of British foreign policy in 1911?
source.model_answer: The speech is exceptionally significant because Lloyd George was a leading radical politician who had previously opposed war; his firm warning demonstrated that the entire British Cabinet was unified in standing militarily with France against German intimidation.

lessons.prologue: By the late nineteenth century, European empires raced to claim colonies across Africa and Asia. When Kaiser Wilhelm II demanded Germany’s 'place in the sun', colonial rivalries erupted into tense showdowns in Morocco. Was imperial greed in distant lands the spark that poisoned European relations before 1914?

sources.title: Source A (Political Cartoon): John Tenniel, "The Greedy Boy" (Punch, 10 January 1885)
sources.caption: John Tenniel's 1885 cartoon for Punch showing German Chancellor Otto von Bismarck carving large slices of colonial pudding ('Angra Pequena' and 'New Guinea'), leaving John Bull with an empty plate following the Berlin Conference.
sources.citation: Punch, or the London Charivari, London (Vol. 88, 10 January 1885, p. 19) / British Cartoon Archive.
sources.context: Published in the British satirical weekly Punch on 10 January 1885 while European diplomats met at Chancellor Otto von Bismarck’s Berlin Conference (1884–1885) during a wave of rival European claims across Africa and the Pacific.
sources.question: What does this cartoon reveal about British reactions to Germany's sudden entry into colonial competition in 1884–1885?
sources.model_answer: The cartoon reveals British resentment and shock at German colonial claims, portraying Bismarck as an aggressive 'greedy boy' taking territories like Angra Pequena and New Guinea that Britain assumed it could dominate without competition.
sources.source_context: Published in the British satirical weekly Punch on 10 January 1885 while European diplomats met at Chancellor Otto von Bismarck’s Berlin Conference (1884–1885) during a wave of rival European claims across Africa and the Pacific.

teacher_notes.source_context: At the 1884–1885 Berlin Conference, Chancellor Bismarck orchestrated the formal partition of Africa, acquiring Germany's first official protectorates in South-West Africa (Angra Pequena/Namibia), Togoland, Cameroon, and German New Guinea. British public opinion was startled by Germany's sudden entry into colonial expansion, portraying Bismarck as a greedy table-companion taking colonial territories Britain considered its natural sphere of influence. **Hinge Question:** How does Tenniel's depiction of Bismarck taking 'Angra Pequena' reveal Britain's resentment when other European powers claimed colonial territory?

sources.title: Source B (Parliamentary Speech): Bernhard von Bülow, Speech on Germany's "Place in the Sun" (1897)
sources.text: The days when Germans abandoned the land to one neighbor and the sea to another, reserving for themselves only the heavens where pure doctrine reigns—those days are over! We do not want to put anyone into the shade, but we too demand our place in the sun (*einen Platz an der Sonne*). In East Asia and Africa, we cannot and will not allow any foreign power to push us aside or monopolize economic trade.
sources.caption: Speech delivered by German Foreign Secretary (later Chancellor) Bernhard von Bülow to the Reichstag in Berlin, inaugurating Germany's aggressive global foreign policy (*Weltpolitik*).
sources.citation: Stenographische Berichte über die Verhandlungen des Deutschen Reichstages, 1897, Vol. 1, p. 60.
sources.context: In 1897, the German government abandoned Bismarck's cautious continental diplomacy in favour of Weltpolitik (world policy), demanding global colonies and prestige equivalent to Britain's.
sources.question: Why did Bernhard von Bülow deliver this speech to the German Reichstag in December 1897?
sources.model_answer: Bülow delivered the speech to rally parliamentary and public support for expanding Germany's colonial empire and navy, declaring that Germany would aggressively challenge existing British and French dominance to secure global prestige.
sources.source_context: In 1897, the German government abandoned Bismarck's cautious continental diplomacy in favour of Weltpolitik (world policy), demanding global colonies and prestige equivalent to Britain's.

teacher_notes.source_context: In 1897, the German government abandoned Bismarck's cautious continental diplomacy in favour of Weltpolitik (world policy), demanding global colonies and prestige equivalent to Britain's. **Hinge Question:** How did the rhetoric of demanding a 'place in the sun' convince other European powers that Germany was no longer a satisfied power, but an aggressive challenger?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: How did the rhetoric of demanding a 'place in the sun' convince other European powers that Germany was no longer a satisfied power, but an aggressive challenger?

sources.title: Source C (Archival Cartography): Walter Crane, Imperial Federation Map of the World (1886)
sources.caption: Walter Crane's iconic 1886 map for The Graphic, illustrating the vast global expanse of the British Empire (shaded in red), Britannia seated on the globe, and imperial statistics compiled by Captain J.C.R. Colomb.
sources.citation: The Graphic, London (24 July 1886) / Norman B. Leventhal Map Center, Boston Public Library (Call No. G3201.F7 1886 .C7).
sources.context: By the late 19th century, Great Britain governed an empire covering approximately a quarter of the globe and one-fifth of the world's population. When Kaiser Wilhelm II and Chancellor Bülow demanded Germany's 'place in the sun' in the late 1890s, they looked with intense envy at British global dominance illustrated in imperial maps like Crane's, feeling that Germany was confined to Central Europe while Britain monopolized global commerce and colonies.
sources.question: What does this map reveal about why Imperial Germany felt 'in the shade' during the late nineteenth-century Scramble for Empire?
sources.model_answer: The map illustrates that the British Empire already encompassed a vast global network across every ocean—including Canada, India, Australia, and key African territories—demonstrating to German leaders that the most valuable colonial and maritime positions were already monopolized by Britain.
sources.source_context: By the late 19th century, Great Britain governed an empire covering approximately a quarter of the globe and one-fifth of the world's population. When Kaiser Wilhelm II and Chancellor Bülow demanded Germany's 'place in the sun' in the late 1890s, they looked with intense envy at British global dominance illustrated in imperial maps like Crane's, feeling that Germany was confined to Central Europe while Britain monopolized global commerce and colonies.

sources.title: Source D (Imperial Telegram): Kaiser Wilhelm II, Telegram from Tangier to Chancellor Bülow (1905)
sources.text: Today I visited the Sultan's representative in Tangier and announced in person that I regard the Sultan of Morocco as an absolutely free and independent sovereign, subject to no foreign control. I declared that Germany insists upon equal commercial rights for all nations, and will never suffer any other power [France] to establish an exclusive protectorate here without international consent.
sources.caption: Kaiser Wilhelm II's official dispatch describing his provocative visit to Tangier, Morocco, designed to test and break the newly signed 1904 Anglo-French Entente Cordiale.
sources.citation: Die Große Politik der Europäischen Kabinette 1871–1914, Vol. 20, Part 2, Document 6589.
sources.context: In 1905, Germany provoked the First Moroccan Crisis by landing Kaiser Wilhelm II at Tangier to champion Moroccan independence against French colonial claims. Germany hoped to expose the 1904 Entente Cordiale as weak; instead, the crisis backfired and drew Britain and France closer together.
sources.question: What does this dispatch reveal about Kaiser Wilhelm II's underlying strategy during the First Moroccan Crisis?
sources.model_answer: The dispatch reveals that the Kaiser used the pretence of Moroccan independence to directly challenge French colonial expansion, aiming to humiliate France and test whether Britain would honour its diplomatic support.
sources.source_context: In 1905, Germany provoked the First Moroccan Crisis by landing Kaiser Wilhelm II at Tangier to champion Moroccan independence against French colonial claims. Germany hoped to expose the 1904 Entente Cordiale as weak; instead, the crisis backfired and drew Britain and France closer together.

teacher_notes.source_context: In 1905, Germany provoked the First Moroccan Crisis by landing Kaiser Wilhelm II at Tangier to champion Moroccan independence against French colonial claims. Germany hoped to expose the 1904 Entente Cordiale as weak; instead, the crisis backfired and drew Britain and France closer together. **Hinge Question:** Why did the Kaiser's dramatic intervention at Tangier ultimately strengthen Anglo-French military cooperation instead of fracturing it?
teacher_notes.hinge_question: Why did the Kaiser's dramatic intervention at Tangier ultimately strengthen Anglo-French military cooperation instead of fracturing it?

sources.title: Source E (Ministerial Speech): David Lloyd George, The Mansion House Speech (21 July 1911)
sources.text: I am also bound to say this: that I believe it is essential in the highest interests, not merely of this country, but of the world, that Britain should at all hazards maintain her place and her prestige amongst the Great Powers of the world... If a situation were to be forced upon us in which peace could only be preserved by the surrender of the great and beneficent position Britain has won with centuries of heroism and achievement, by allowing Britain to be treated where her interests were vitally affected as if she didn't count in the Cabinet of Nations, then I say emphatically that peace at that price would be a humiliation intolerable for a great country like ours to endure.
sources.caption: David Lloyd George addressing the annual Bankers' Dinner at Mansion House, delivering an unambiguous public warning to Germany following the dispatch of the gunboat Panther to Agadir.
sources.citation: The Times (London), 22 July 1911, p. 7; Hansard Parliamentary Debates.
sources.context: During the Second Moroccan Crisis (1911), Chancellor David Lloyd George—previously regarded as a pacifist-leaning Radical—delivered a blistering public warning that Britain would fight rather than allow Germany to bully France or threaten maritime routes.
sources.question: What makes Lloyd George's Mansion House speech particularly significant as evidence of British foreign policy in 1911?
sources.model_answer: The speech is exceptionally significant because Lloyd George was a leading radical politician who had previously opposed war; his firm warning demonstrated that the entire British Cabinet was unified in standing militarily with France against German intimidation.
sources.source_context: During the Second Moroccan Crisis (1911), Chancellor David Lloyd George—previously regarded as a pacifist-leaning Radical—delivered a blistering public warning that Britain would fight rather than allow Germany to bully France or threaten maritime routes.

stages.title: The British Two-Power Standard

stages.title: Tirpitz's Naval Laws & Risk Fleet
stages.trigger: Germany passes Naval Laws to build 38 modern battleships directly facing Britain across the North Sea.
stages.connective: Britain viewed the German fleet as an existential threat to its survival, destroying Anglo-German diplomatic friendship.
stages.question: How did Admiral von Tirpitz’s 1898 "Risk Theory" threaten Britain?

stages.title: The Dreadnought Revolution
stages.trigger: Britain launches HMS Dreadnought, armed with ten 12-inch guns and steam turbines, rendering all previous battleships instantly obsolete.
stages.connective: Because older battleships were now obsolete, the naval race reset to zero: Germany rushed to build its own dreadnoughts.
stages.question: Why did launching HMS Dreadnought in 1906 wipe out Britain’s lead?

stages.title: The 1909 British Naval Panic
stages.trigger: Amid fears Germany was secretly building dreadnoughts faster than Britain, the British public and press chant: "We want eight and we won't wait!"
stages.connective: Forced the British government to double its naval construction, spending vast sums to maintain its lead over Germany.
stages.question: Why did British crowds chant "We want eight and we won’t wait" in 1909?

stages.title: Haldane Mission Failure & Redeployment
stages.trigger: Talks for a naval truce collapse when Germany demands British neutrality in any European war; Britain redeploys its fleet to the North Sea.

A large German army on land was a continental concern; a large German battle fleet stationed hours across the North Sea was an immediate dagger pointed at Britain's throat.
